title: “THERE IS NOW NO CONDEMNATION”—BUT JESUS NEVER SAID THERE IS NOW NO NEED FOR REPENTANCE
paragraphs: “THERE IS NOW NO CONDEMNATION”—BUT JESUS NEVER SAID THERE IS NOW NO NEED FOR REPENTANCE

Romans 8:1 may be one of the most comforting sentences ever written to a guilty human heart. It may also be one of the most dangerously misunderstood. Grace does not give sin permission to stay. Grace gives sinners a Savior powerful enough to bring them home.
There is a sentence in the Bible that people reach for when shame becomes unbearable.
When the memories come back.
When the temptation won again.
When you promised God, “Never again,” and somehow found yourself standing in the wreckage of another again.
When everybody at church thinks you are doing well, but you know what happened when nobody was watching.
When your Bible is open but your conscience is screaming.
When you wonder whether God is tired of forgiving you.
Then you remember the words:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
And suddenly you can breathe.
But then another danger appears.
Because the same verse that can rescue a repentant sinner from crushing despair can be twisted into an excuse for an unrepentant sinner to remain comfortable in rebellion.
No condemnation.
Does that mean no consequences?
No repentance?
No war against sin?
No obedience?
Can I knowingly continue embracing what Christ died to save me from and simply whisper, “Grace”?
Paul’s answer is devastatingly clear.
No.
And understanding why may completely change the way you hear Romans 8:1.
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Ouden ara nyn katakrima tois en Christō Iēsou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say there is now no condemnation for sin.
He does not announce that evil has become harmless.
He does not declare repentance obsolete.
He does not say holiness no longer matters.
The breathtaking promise belongs to those who are ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou — “in Christ Jesus.”
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of sinners discovering a theological loophole.
It is the story of condemned sinners being united to a crucified and risen Savior.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years confusing two completely different voices.
One voice says:
“You sinned. Run away from God. Hide. You are filthy. There is no hope for someone like you.”
The other says:
“You sinned. Come into the light. Confess it. Turn from it. Run to Christ. His mercy is greater than your failure.”
Those voices are not the same.
Condemnation drives you toward hopelessness.
Godly conviction drives you toward repentance.
One whispers, “There is no way home.”
The Gospel announces, “The way home has a name.”
Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:1 does not float by itself in the Bible.
There is a “therefore” at the beginning because Paul has already taken us somewhere.
He has taken us through the courtroom.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23.
He has taken us to the horrifying wages of rebellion.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23.
He has taken us into the strange battlefield of the human heart where someone can recognize what is right and still experience the terrible power of indwelling sin.
Then near the end of Romans 7 comes the cry:
“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
Listen carefully to the question.
Paul does not ask:
What rule will save me?
What excuse will save me?
What religious performance will save me?
He asks:
Who?
And the answer comes immediately:
“I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Then Romans 8 explodes into view.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
Why?
Not because sin stopped being serious.
Because Jesus became the sinner’s substitute.
The Gospel does not say God looked at our rebellion and decided it did not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin mattered enough that redemption required the blood of Christ.
God did not save us by pretending justice did not exist.
At the cross, mercy and justice meet in Jesus Christ.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the suffering Servant:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Vehu mecholal mipsha‘einu.
“He was wounded for our transgressions…” — Isaiah 53:5.
The Hebrew מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ — mipsha‘einu points to our transgressions, our rebellions.
Ours.
That is the scandal.
The innocent Christ suffers for guilty people.
The righteous One receives what rebels deserve so rebels united to Him can receive what they could never earn.
That is grace.
But grace becomes grotesquely distorted when we turn the wounds of Jesus into permission to keep loving the sins for which He was wounded.
Paul anticipated that distortion long before any of us made it.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” — Romans 6:1.
His response in Greek is wonderfully forceful:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
It carries the force of:
Absolutely not. May it never be.
Then Paul asks:
“How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” — Romans 6:2.
That does not mean genuine Christians instantly become incapable of sin.
The New Testament would make little sense if it did.
Believers still stumble.
Believers still need confession.
Believers still need correction.
Believers still fight desires they wish would disappear overnight.
First John tells Christians:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9.
So the question is not whether a Christian ever falls.
The deeper question is:
What do you do when you fall?
Do you defend the darkness?
Or drag it into the light?
Do you rename sin so you can keep it?
Or confess sin because you want Christ more than you want your chains?
Do you use grace to silence conviction?
Or does grace make you want to run back into the arms of the One you have grieved?
There is an enormous difference between a believer struggling against sin and a person making peace with sin.
A struggling Christian may fall repeatedly and hate the fall.
A hardened heart eventually begins furnishing the prison cell.
It puts pictures on the walls.
Makes excuses comfortable.
Changes the vocabulary.
Calls bondage “freedom.”
Calls compromise “being authentic.”
Calls biblical correction “judgment.”
And eventually may use the blood of Jesus as theological camouflage for refusing the lordship of Jesus.
That is not what “no condemnation” means.
Grace is not God saying:
“Your sin does not matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“Your sin was so serious that My Son went to the cross—and My love is so astonishing that I gave Him for sinners like you.”
Keep reading Romans 8.
Paul says:
“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.” — Romans 8:2.
Free.
But free from what?
Not free to sin without concern.
Free from the dominion that once held us.
Later Paul writes:
That is not permission.
That is warfare.
And maybe that is what somebody needed to hear today.
You have mistaken struggling for hypocrisy.
You have assumed that because temptation still knocks, Christ must have abandoned the house.
You have hated yourself because the battle is still happening.
But the existence of battle is not necessarily evidence that God has left you.
Sometimes the battle exists precisely because surrender to sin is no longer acceptable to you.
Before Christ, darkness can feel like home.
When Christ begins transforming us, darkness increasingly feels like a prison.
You may still stumble into what once enslaved you.
But now something inside cries:
I don't want to live here anymore.
That cry matters.
Not because it earns salvation.
Jesus alone saves.
But because the Holy Spirit does not merely comfort God's children in sin. He transforms God's children toward the likeness of Christ.
So hear this carefully if you failed last night.
If you returned to pornography.
If anger controlled you again.
If pride poisoned another relationship.
If greed has quietly become your master.
If jealousy is eating you alive.
If you lied.
If you betrayed somebody.
If alcohol, lust, bitterness, gossip, dishonesty, envy, or secret compromise has become the room nobody is allowed to enter.
Do not hear Romans 8:1 saying:
Stay there.
Hear it saying:
Because of Christ, you can come out of hiding.
There is a world of difference.
Satan would love to push you toward either of two cliffs.
On one side:
Despair.
“You have sinned too badly. Jesus doesn't want you anymore.”
On the other:
Presumption.
“Sin all you want. Jesus doesn't care.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
To despair, the Gospel says:
Look at the cross. His grace is greater than your record.
To presumption, the Gospel says:
Look at the cross. Your sin is more serious than you imagined.
And to both, Jesus says:
Come to Me.
The cross is where our excuses die without our hope dying with them.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not purchasing God's forgiveness with enough tears.
It is not self-punishment.
It is not trying to make yourself miserable enough that God finally decides you have suffered sufficiently.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of changing one's mind or turning in response to truth.
Biblical repentance involves a real turning toward God.
We stop defending what He calls sin.
We agree with Him.
We bring it into the light.
We turn toward Christ.
And even repentance itself does not become a medal we hold up before God and say, “See? Now I deserve You.”
No.
Empty hands.
That is how sinners come.
Empty hands.
Nothing to boast about.
Nothing to negotiate with.
Nothing but need.
And Christ.
Perhaps your greatest problem today is not that you think too little of grace.
Perhaps you have never realized how radical grace actually is.
Cheap grace says:
Jesus forgives me, therefore I don't have to change.
Biblical grace says:
Jesus has forgiven and claimed me, therefore I no longer want sin to remain my master.
Cheap grace asks:
How close can I get to sin without losing heaven?
Love asks:
How close can I get to Jesus?
That question exposes us.
Because sometimes we don't really want freedom from sin.
We want freedom from consequences.
We want Jesus to remove hell while leaving our idols untouched.
We want a Savior who forgives but never interrupts.
A King who never commands.
A Shepherd who never redirects.
A Physician who diagnoses nothing.
A cross without dying to self.
A resurrection without a grave.
But the Jesus of Scripture does not merely offer us improved circumstances.
He gives us Himself.
And when Christ takes hold of a human life, He does not simply rewrite its destination.
He begins rewriting the person.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Maybe your story contains chapters you desperately wish could be deleted.
Sexual sin.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Abortion.
Infidelity.
Years of unbelief.
Religious hypocrisy.
A ruined friendship.
A wounded child.
A wounded parent.
A secret habit.
Something you did.
Something you became.
Something you still cannot say aloud.
You cannot travel backward and prevent those pages from being written.
But Jesus Christ specializes in stories human beings would have thrown away.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The woman of Samaria carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Christ reached the end of his life with nothing left to offer.
The Gospel is filled with people whose histories should have disqualified them from boasting.
And that is precisely the point.
Grace leaves no room for boasting.
Your scandal does not become beautiful because the sin was beautiful.
Sin destroys.
The beauty is that Jesus can enter what sin destroyed and write redemption where we expected only an ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the final word.
Maybe you need to stop running today.
Not tomorrow.
Today.
Stop rehearsing your defense.
Stop blaming everybody else.
Stop calling bondage personality.
Stop waiting until you “feel spiritual enough” to return.
Come filthy if you are filthy.
Come ashamed if you are ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come exhausted.
Come with the confession you have been terrified to speak.
But come to Jesus.
“If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7.
Did you see it?
Walking in the light does not mean pretending you never needed cleansing.
It means you stop hiding from the One whose blood cleanses.
Somebody reading this has been punishing themselves for something Christ is calling them to confess and surrender.
You think hating yourself proves that you understand the seriousness of your sin.
But self-hatred cannot atone for you.
Shame cannot crucify itself for you.
Regret cannot rise from the dead.
Jesus already went to the cross.
Jesus already entered the grave.
Jesus already rose.
And if your faith is in Him, your hope is not that you have finally become good enough to escape condemnation.
Your hope is Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
Now.
What a word.
Not after you have spent twenty years compensating for your past.
Not after everybody you disappointed finally approves of you again.
Not after you have punished yourself adequately.
Now.
For those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is justification.
The believer's right standing before God rests on Christ, not on a flawless record of personal performance.
But the Christ who justifies also transforms.
Sanctification does not purchase justification, but justification is never meant to become an excuse for despising sanctification.
We are not saved because we became holy enough.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, and the God who saves His people begins making them holy.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
But do not stop before Paul's next sentence:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” — Ephesians 2:8–10.
Grace saves.
Grace changes.
Grace forgives.
Grace disciplines.
Grace receives prodigals.
Grace teaches prodigals that the pigpen was never home.
So when temptation whispers tonight:
“No condemnation. Go ahead.”
Answer it with the rest of Scripture.
No condemnation does not mean sin has become my friend.
It means sin no longer gets to condemn the one whose condemnation Christ bore.
And because Jesus purchased me at such a cost, I do not want to turn His wounds into permission to return willingly to the chains from which He is freeing me.
And when you fail—and believers sometimes grievously fail—do not let the enemy rewrite Romans 8:1 in the opposite direction.
Do not hear:
“There is now condemnation because you stumbled.”
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help when needed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Put boundaries around recurring temptation.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
Get back into Scripture.
Pray even when prayer feels embarrassing.
And run toward Jesus instead of away from Him.
The same Peter who denied Christ three times was restored by Christ.
Failure did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe there is something between you and God that has remained unnamed for too long.
You know what it is.
I don't.
The person sitting beside you may not.
But you know.
And God knows.
So be honest.
Has “grace” become the word you use when you do not want to surrender something?
Or has “condemnation” become the prison you remain inside because you cannot believe Christ could truly forgive somebody with your history?
Whichever side you are standing on, the road leads to the same Person.
Jesus.
Repent and come.
Believe and come.
Broken, come.
Ashamed, come.
Tired of fighting, come.
Tired of pretending, come.
There is no salvation hidden inside your performance.
There is no salvation hidden inside your rebellion either.
Salvation is in Christ.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who keeps smiling while falling apart.
The Christian who thinks another failure means God could never receive them again.
The person using grace to justify chains that are quietly destroying them.
The son.
The daughter.
The husband.
The wife.
The old friend you haven't spoken to in months.
Send this to them privately if that would be wiser.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when Romans 8:1 is no longer theology you are discussing.
It will be oxygen you need.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a way to purchase God's favor.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness is not merchandise.
Jesus Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
Because someday the sentence that matters most will not be the sentence shame wrote about you.
Not the sentence your past wrote.
Not the sentence people wrote after seeing your worst moment.
Not even the sentence you have repeated to yourself for years.
For everyone who is truly in Christ, another verdict has already thundered from the Gospel:
No condemnation.
Not permission to return to the grave.
Permission to stop living as though the grave still owns you.
So repent without running from Him.
Fight sin without believing your fighting earns His love.
Confess without pretending.
Obey without boasting.
Get up when you fall.
Walk in the light.
And when shame reaches for the pen again, remember who holds the final page.
Your worst chapter may explain why you came to Jesus—but it does not get to decide how Jesus finishes your story.
